```{r}
#| label: setup
library(ggcarto)
library(ggplot2)
library(sf)
cty <- northeast_counties
```

ggcarto reports a lot of numbers: a *fit* of 0.89, a *smallest class* of
2.4%, a *dE* of 7.8, a *contrast ratio* of 1.03. This document says what
each one is for. It starts from what a choropleth map has to do for its
reader, states the conventions cartographers have settled on for doing it,
and then names the function and the metric that checks each convention.
Read it once and the printed reports will make sense; keep the checklist at
the end.

## What the reader is doing

A person reading a choropleth is doing three things, in this order: finding
the areas that are dark (or light), matching a colour on the map back to a
row of the legend, and then reading that row as a sentence about the world:
"these counties have unemployment above 6%". Every design decision either
helps one of those three tasks or gets in its way.

Colour is the weakest visual channel we have for reading numbers; position
and length are far better [@cleveland1984]. On a map, position is spent on
geography, so colour is all that is left, and the map should ask it to carry
as little as possible. That is the argument for classing a continuous
variable into a handful of ordered colours, and for keeping the handful
small.

## How many classes

**The convention.** Three to seven classes for a sequential (single-hue,
light-to-dark) scheme; five is the usual choice. With fewer than three the
map shows no pattern; above seven, readers can no longer match a colour on
the map back to the legend reliably, especially on small polygons and in
print [@slocum2009; @brewer2016]. A diverging scheme wants an odd number, so
there is a neutral middle class sitting on the midpoint.

**What ggcarto measures.** `class_guide()` evaluates each candidate count on
four things and prints them side by side:

| Column | What it is | How to read it |
|---|---|---|
| `fit` | Goodness of variance fit, $1 - SSW/SST$: the share of the variable's variance that lies *between* classes rather than *within* them [@jenks1971]. 0 for one class, 1 when every class is constant. | How faithfully the classes reproduce the distribution. Above 0.80 is the usual floor for a natural-breaks map. It is the criterion Fisher-Jenks optimises, so it means most for that family; for `quantile` it is only descriptive. |
| `gain` | The increase in fit over the previous candidate. | Where gains fall under 0.05 the curve has flattened and another class is buying legend length, not information. |
| `smallest class` | Share of observations in the least-populated class. | A class under 2% is a colour the reader will hunt for; under 3 observations it is a legend key for one or two polygons. |
| `readability` | A rating by count alone: up to 5 excellent, 6 good, 7 fair, 8+ poor. | The perceptual ceiling, independent of the data. |

The suggestion is a rule applied to those columns (the rules are in
`?class_guide`), and it is called a *suggestion* because there is no
optimum: fit rises with every added class, forever, and only judgement
decides where to stop.

```{r}
#| label: guide
class_guide(cty$median_income, "fisher")
```

```{r}
#| label: guide-plot
#| fig-height: 4.6
plot(class_guide(cty$median_income, "fisher"))
```

## Where the breaks fall

**The convention.** The classification method is an argument about what
the map is for, not a setting [@monmonier2018]. Natural breaks (`fisher`)
follow the gaps in the data and give the best single map. Quantiles give
every class the same number of areas, which makes the map balanced and the
legend readable as "top fifth"; Brewer and Pickle found readers answered
questions about quantile maps most accurately [@brewer2002]. Equal intervals
are honest about magnitude and fail on skewed data. Standard-deviation
classes answer "above or below average". Fixed breaks are for thresholds
that mean something outside the data, and for series of maps that must be
comparable.

**What ggcarto measures.** `class_summary()` shows the count and share in
every class, the observed minimum and maximum inside each, and the label the
legend will carry. `plot_breaks()` and `compare_breaks()` put the breaks on
the histogram, which is the quickest way to see a method fail. Three
things to look for:

* **Empty or thin classes.** A legend row with no area on the map, or almost
  none. Equal intervals on a skewed variable produce them reliably.
* **Breaks too close together.** Two cut points within 1% of the range draw
  a distinction the data cannot support; quantiles on a variable with a
  spike produce them.
* **Where a value on the break goes.** With a break at 10, is 10 "under 10"
  or "10 and above"? ggplot2 and ggcarto default to `(a, b]` -- 10 goes
  below; classInt and tmap default to `[a, b)`. `closure = "left"` and
  `as_count = TRUE` make the choice explicit, and `class_summary()` shows the
  consequence.

```{r}
#| label: compare
#| fig-height: 5
compare_breaks(cty$pop, c("equal", "quantile", "fisher"), n = 5, log_x = TRUE)
```

## Colour

**The convention.** Three kinds of palette, for three kinds of data
[@brewer1994; @harrower2003]. *Sequential*: one hue running light to dark,
for an ordered variable with a low and a high; darker means more. *Diverging*:
two hues meeting at a neutral, for an ordered variable with a meaningful
middle -- zero change, the regional average, 50% -- and the neutral must sit
on that middle. *Qualitative*: distinct hues at similar lightness, for
categories with no order, never for a number. The lightness ramp is what
carries the value; hue is decoration. Roughly one man in twelve has a
red-green deficiency, so a palette has to survive that [@borland2007;
@crameri2020].

**What ggcarto measures.** `check_palette()` reports, and `diagnose_map()`
repeats for the palette actually on the map:

| Measure | What it is | Threshold |
|---|---|---|
| Lightness | CIELAB $L^*$ of every class, 0 (black) to 100 (white). | Sequential palettes must run one way; diverging ones must be lightest (or darkest) in the middle with both ends darker. |
| Centre chroma | Colourfulness of the middle class of a diverging palette. | Above 15, the "neutral" centre is not neutral and readers will not see it as zero. |
| Adjacent dE | CIE76 colour difference between neighbouring classes. | Under 10 the two are hard to tell apart on small polygons; under 5 they are effectively one class. |
| Colour vision | The same differences after simulating deuteranopia, protanopia and tritanopia (colorspace); adjacent *and* non-adjacent pairs, because on a map the classes are not lined up. | Under 10, that share of readers loses the distinction. |
| Contrast | WCAG luminance ratio of each class against the background. | Under 1.2 the class vanishes into the page; trim the pale end with `range = c(0.15, 1)` or draw outlines. |
| NA distance | dE between the missing-data colour and the nearest class. | Under 10, "no data" reads as a value. |

```{r}
#| label: palette
check_palette("brewer::YlGnBu", 5, na.value = "grey85")
```

```{r}
#| label: palette-plot
#| fig-height: 3.4
plot_palette("brewer::RdYlGn", 7)
```

Two habits worth adopting before any of that: reverse a palette that runs
dark-to-light (several viridis palettes do), because a choropleth is read as
*more ink means more*; and never put a diverging palette on a map without a
`midpoint`.

## The legend

**The convention.** The legend is where a colour becomes a sentence, so it
should read like one. Ranges, not bare break values ("$54,000 to $64,000",
not "64,000"). Rounded numbers; nobody needs $64,528 in a legend
[@brewer2016]. Units on the numbers. Open end classes when the data extremes
are not meaningful numbers: "Under $54,000" is a fact about the world,
"$39,717 to $54,000" is a fact about the dataset. A key for missing data,
in a colour that cannot be mistaken for a low value. For a bivariate map,
the legend is a grid, sits close to the map, and names both variables and
their direction; and no more than a 3 x 3 or 4 x 4 grid, because nine or
sixteen colours is the limit of what readers can match [@stevens2015].

**What ggcarto does.** `label_map()` writes the labels (`style =
"interval"`, `open`, `prefix`, `suffix`, `big.mark`, `digits`, `scale`);
`na_key()` adds the missing-data key that ggplot2's binned and continuous
legends cannot draw; `legend_bivariate()` draws the grid, with `counts =
TRUE` to show an empty cell; `diagnose_map()` prints the labels the legend
will actually carry, so a typo or a wrong unit is caught before the map
leaves the screen.

## Outliers, limits and missing data

**The convention.** An outlier should not be allowed to stretch the ramp so
that every other area shares one colour. The cartographic treatment is to
*squish*: clamp values beyond the limits into the end classes and say so in
the legend ("$110,000 and above"), rather than drop them as if they were
missing. Missing data get their own neutral colour and their own key.

**What ggcarto measures.** `diagnose_map()` counts the values outside the
limits (below and above), says whether they were squished or censored, and
flags when more than 5% of the areas have been clamped -- at that share the
map is hiding real variation and the legend must say so. It counts missing
values and checks their colour against the classes. `trim_limits()` sets
limits from quantiles of the data (not the range: ggplot2 would otherwise
hand a limits function only the minimum and maximum).

```{r}
#| label: diagnose
p <- ggplot(cty) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = pct_poverty), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  scale_fill_intervals("brewer::YlOrRd", "fisher", 5, range = c(0.15, 1),
                       na.value = "grey85",
                       labels = label_map(style = "interval", suffix = "%",
                                          digits = 0, open = TRUE)) +
  na_key("No data") +
  theme_ggcarto()
diagnose_map(p)
```

## Layout

These are not measured -- they are the part a person still has to do -- but
they are where most maps go wrong.

* **Projection.** A choropleth compares areas, so use an equal-area
  projection (Albers for a region, `sf::st_transform()`); `northeast_counties`
  ships in one. Never plot raw longitude/latitude for a choropleth.
* **Size and aspect.** Let the region set the aspect ratio and make the map
  the largest thing on the page. For a report figure, 7 x 5 inches at 150
  dpi; for a slide, 10 x 5.6. A map that has to be read on a phone needs
  fewer classes, not smaller text.
* **Text.** A base size of 11 pt for print, 12 to 14 for screens; legend
  text no smaller than 8 pt. Title in the darkest ink, subtitle and legend in
  a grey a step lighter, source and notes in a lighter grey still. Say what,
  where and when in the title and subtitle; say where the data came from in
  the caption.
* **Borders.** Thin white or off-white polygon outlines (`linewidth = 0.1`)
  separate neighbouring areas of the same class without adding a colour.
  Drop them entirely at very small sizes.
* **Background.** White, and nothing else on the page but the map, its
  title, its legend and its source: colour is spent on the data. Trim the
  palest class with `range = c(0.15, 1)` or give it an outline so it does
  not vanish into the page. That restraint, and the text hierarchy above,
  is what `theme_ggcarto()` sets.
* **Legend placement.** Under the map, in a row, for a wide region like the
  Northeast; to the right for a tall one. A bivariate legend is inset on the
  map, in an empty corner (`inset_legend()`).

```{r}
#| label: layout
#| fig-height: 5.6
ggplot(cty) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = median_income), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  scale_fill_intervals("brewer::YlGnBu", "fisher", 5, range = c(0.15, 1),
                       labels = label_map(style = "interval", prefix = "$",
                                          scale = 1/1000, suffix = "k", digits = 0,
                                          open = TRUE)) +
  labs(title = "Median household income, 2015-2019",
       subtitle = "Counties of the US Northeast. Five natural-breaks classes; the top class\nstarts where the suburbs of Boston, New York and Philadelphia do.",
       caption = "Source: American Community Survey 5-year estimates, via the usdata package. Albers equal-area projection.",
       fill = NULL) +
  theme_ggcarto()
```

## The checklist

Before a map leaves your hands:

1. `class_guide()` -- is the number of classes defensible, and can you say
   why you chose it?
2. `class_summary()` -- does every class hold enough areas; do the labels
   read as sentences with units?
3. `plot_breaks()` -- do the breaks fall where the data have structure, or
   where the method's arithmetic put them?
4. `check_palette()` -- right kind of palette for the variable; classes
   distinguishable, with and without colour-vision deficiency; palest class
   visible; missing-data colour distinct.
5. `diagnose_map()` -- the finished map: nothing flagged that you cannot
   explain.
6. The map itself: equal-area projection, a title that says what, where and
   when, a source, a legend the reader can read as a sentence, a key for
   missing data.
